title: Ask me anything – Allen & Overy adopts ChatGPT-style legal AI tool
author: Dan Bindman

dom.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The report supports Harvey as an early test case for workflow-oriented legal AI, documenting substantial firm-wide use and expectations of transformed, more efficient delivery. It also aligns with the synthesis’s caution that current systems are augmentation tools whose outputs require human verification; it does not establish autonomous agentic delivery, realised savings or durable vendor advantage.
qs: Some 3,500 lawyers asked Harvey about 40,000 questions for their day-to-day client work.
An A&O spokesman stressed that the software did not aim to replace lawyers and that Harvey’s results needed to be carefully assessed for accuracy.

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: The source supports Harvey’s strategy through its description of a natural-language interface for existing legal workflows and A&O’s first-mover partnership. It also aligns with the copilot framing by presenting Harvey as augmenting rather than replacing lawyers. Consistent with the synthesis, however, it provides stakeholder expectations rather than measured evidence of accuracy, productivity, intensive use or governance effectiveness.
qs: In an email interview with US website Techcrunch following that news, Harvey co-founder Gabriel Pereya said: “Our product provides lawyers with a natural language interface for their existing legal workflows.
Mr Pereyra said the aim was not to replace lawyers, but for Harvey to serve as an intermediary between tech and lawyer, or a “natural language interface to the law”.

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s core expectation that Harvey can augment lawyers, improve legal-service delivery and redirect time toward higher-value work. However, it offers predictions tied to product capabilities and partnership rather than evidence that sustained use, workflow redesign or implementation support has produced organisational value.
qs: “Harvey will make lawyers more efficient, allowing them to produce higher-quality work and spend more time on the high-value parts of their job,” he said.
Harvey AI is not just another platform, but a game-changer that will enable us to deliver unprecedented value, efficiency and innovation to our clients.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by documenting substantial enterprise adoption and anticipated efficiency gains while not treating usage, funding or optimistic forecasts as proof of accuracy, realised savings or durable defensibility. It expressly preserves human verification as a condition of use.

kp.k: Firmwide adoption follows substantial trial usage
kp.d: Bindman reports that Allen & Overy became the first law firm to adopt a ChatGPT-style AI assistant to accelerate work for more than 3,500 lawyers. In the trial beginning in November 2022, some 3,500 lawyers asked approximately 40,000 questions for day-to-day client work. Markets innovation head David Wakeling described the results as “amazing”; the reported usage figures establish adoption activity, rather than quantified improvements in accuracy or productivity.
qs: Global law firm Allen & Overy (A&O) has become the first law firm to adopt an artificial intelligence (AI) assistant similar to ChatGPT to help speed up the work of more than 3,500 lawyers, which could save the firm millions of pounds.
The firm’s trial of the system since last November had shown “amazing results”, he said.
Some 3,500 lawyers asked Harvey about 40,000 questions for their day-to-day client work.

kp.k: Natural-language instructions support research, drafting and document revision
kp.d: The article describes Harvey as multilingual software using natural language processing, machine learning and data analytics. In comments originally given to Techcrunch and reproduced here, Harvey's co-founder describes a natural-language interface to existing legal workflows, allowing lawyers to request research or document changes rather than perform them manually. The lease-clause example illustrates an intended capability, not a reported performance test.
qs: It uses natural language processing, machine learning and data analytics to automate and enhance different aspects of legal work. It can operate in multiple languages.
“Instead of manually editing legal documents or performing legal research, Harvey enables lawyers to describe the task they wish to accomplish in simple instructions and receive the generated result.
“To enable this, Harvey leverages large language models to both understand users’ intent and to generate the correct output.”
For example, a lawyer could ask: “Tell me if this clause in a lease is in violation of California law, and if so, rewrite it so it is no longer in violation”.

kp.d: An A&O spokesman frames Harvey as an initial research and drafting tool, not a replacement for lawyers, and explicitly requires careful assessment of output accuracy. Harvey's co-founder likewise presents it as an intermediary between lawyers and technology. These statements describe an assisted workflow retaining lawyer involvement rather than autonomous reliance on generated results.
qs: An A&O spokesman stressed that the software did not aim to replace lawyers and that Harvey’s results needed to be carefully assessed for accuracy.
It was an initial research and drafting tool which, when used properly, could save lawyers a few hours a week each.
Mr Pereyra said the aim was not to replace lawyers, but for Harvey to serve as an intermediary between tech and lawyer, or a “natural language interface to the law”.

kp.k: Small individual time savings could produce large firm savings
kp.d: The A&O spokesman estimates that proper use could save each lawyer a few hours weekly and argues that these modest individual savings aggregate into significant cost savings at a large firm. The article suggests savings could reach millions of pounds, while the spokesman predicts greater financial benefits as Harvey becomes faster. These are conditional estimates and forecasts, not reported realised savings.
qs: It was an initial research and drafting tool which, when used properly, could save lawyers a few hours a week each.
But the spokesman pointed out that, in such a large firm, small savings of time amounted to a significant cost saving overall.
As time went on, Harvey would speed up, making the financial benefit greater.

kp.k: Firm and vendor anticipate higher-value legal work
kp.d: A&O says Harvey could derive insights, recommendations and predictions from large datasets to improve client service. Harvey's co-founder predicts increased efficiency, higher-quality work and more lawyer time devoted to high-value tasks. These are attributed expectations about service quality and work allocation, rather than measured client outcomes.
qs: A&O said Harvey could help generate insights, recommendations and predictions based on large volumes of data, “enabling lawyers to deliver faster, smarter and more cost-effective solutions to their clients”.
“Harvey will make lawyers more efficient, allowing them to produce higher-quality work and spend more time on the high-value parts of their job,” he said.

kp.k: OpenAI backing accompanies predictions of changed lawyer time allocation
kp.d: The article reports that Harvey received $5m from OpenAI in November 2022. Brad Lightcap, who runs the OpenAI Startup Fund backing Harvey, explains the investment through a belief that AI could profoundly affect legal processes and fundamentally change how lawyers spend their time. This is an investor's rationale and prediction, distinct from the reported funding event.
qs: Last November, Harvey received $5m in funding from OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT.

Brad Lightcap, who runs the OpenAI Startup Fund backing Harvey, said: “We invested in Harvey because we believe AI can have a profound impact on the legal process and their proprietary platform will fundamentally change the way lawyers spend their time.”

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Harvey is presented as a lawyer-assistance tool that accelerates research and drafting, potentially creating substantial aggregate savings rather than replacing lawyers.
pts.d: Bindman reports A&O's adoption of Harvey to accelerate work for more than 3,500 lawyers and describes millions of pounds in savings as a possibility, not a realised result. An unnamed A&O spokesman says proper use could save each lawyer a few hours weekly and that savings across a large firm would be significant. The spokesman predicts further financial benefits as Harvey becomes faster, while stressing that lawyers must verify accuracy and that replacement is not the aim.

pts.k: Natural-language task instructions and analysis of large datasets are claimed to improve legal workflows, work quality and client service.
pts.d: A&O says Harvey could generate insights, recommendations and predictions from large datasets, enabling faster and more cost-effective client solutions. Harvey co-founder Gabriel Pereyra describes lawyers requesting research or document editing in ordinary language and receiving generated results. His lease-clause example illustrates an intended capability, rather than a documented test result. He predicts greater efficiency, higher-quality work and more time for high-value tasks. Bindman also reports multilingual operation.

pts.k: Firm leaders and Harvey's investor predict broader transformation of legal services and lawyers' allocation of time.
pts.d: A&O markets innovation head David Wakeling characterises Harvey as potentially transformative for the industry. Senior partner Wim Dejonghe predicts exceptional client value, efficiency and innovation. OpenAI Startup Fund head Brad Lightcap expresses an investment belief that Harvey will fundamentally alter how lawyers spend their time. These are broad expectations, not quantified industry outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The main empirical basis is reported trial usage; benefits are supported by participant assessments and stakeholder statements rather than measured performance results.
pts.d: The article reports approximately 3,500 lawyers asking about 40,000 questions during A&O's trial for day-to-day client work. Wakeling's assessment supplies qualitative experience. The usage counts establish trial scale but are not measurements of accuracy, hours saved, work quality or financial returns. The article supplies no benchmark, comparative study or savings calculation. Pereyra's workflow account is a product description, while Dejonghe's and Lightcap's statements express expectations. OpenAI's $5m funding is reported as investment context, not performance evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Adoption is reported in February 2023 following a trial beginning in November 2022; projected savings require proper use and accuracy checks, with no deadline for wider transformation.
pts.d: The article is dated 16 February 2023, making 'last November' November 2022. Weekly time savings are conditional estimates for initial research and drafting, not reported measured gains. Human verification qualifies the assistance model. Greater financial benefits are predicted as the tool speeds up, but without a specified schedule. Claims about higher quality, client value and industry transformation are forward-looking and undated.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate beneficiaries identified are A&O lawyers, the firm and its clients; broader claims extend to lawyers and the legal industry.
pts.d: A&O lawyers are expected to spend less time on initial research and drafting and more on high-value work, while retaining responsibility for assessing output accuracy. A&O is expected to benefit financially from aggregating small individual time savings across its large workforce. Clients are promised faster, smarter, more cost-effective service and greater value. Pereyra and Lightcap extend the time-allocation claims to lawyers generally, while A&O leaders predict industry-wide change. The source does not specify effects by seniority, quantify staffing changes or discuss access to justice.
